sheet-72-1.description: The upper strip of sheet 72 of the 1907 New Jersey Coast volume shows Highland Beach, the resort at the north end of the Sea Bright barrier where the wooden County Bridge crossed the Shrewsbury River from the Highlands. The sheet is turned on the page: Ocean Avenue runs left to right with north towards the right, the Shrewsbury River along the top and the Atlantic Ocean along the bottom, and a compass rose near the ocean edge. On the river side of Ocean Avenue stand the Surf House and its pavilion beside a basin, cottages of the Highland Beach Improvement Company, and, east of the bridge abutment, a resort complex enclosed by a dashed line: beer storage, water closets, a photo gallery, an open platform, a pavilion, an open second-storey bathing pavilion and two long rows of bath houses on piles, fronted by a board walk. A pier runs out into the river, and at the right a steam boat dock is flanked by rows of cottages on posts, including two Twin Light cottages, an ice house and the Melrah Club. Between Ocean Avenue and the ocean bulkhead lie bowling alleys and the double track of the Central Railroad of New Jersey, marked as continuing to Sandy Hook, with a road branching off at the right edge. Block numbers 184 and 185 and house numbers 2908 and 2910 are printed along the avenue. A six-inch water pipe runs in the avenue. The left end continues the lower strip of the same sheet; the inset of the Neptune Boat Club at the upper left is a separate part and lies outside this one.
notes: Ocean Avenue here is today's NJ 36 / Ocean Avenue; the modern road appears to run on the line of the former Central Railroad of New Jersey tracks, about 10 m east of the 1907 avenue.
The County Bridge (wooden) is the predecessor of the NJ 36 Highlands bridge; the modern bridge crosses the river on nearly the same line before curving south to Ocean Avenue.
An unnamed road labelled only "Road" leaves Ocean Avenue at the right edge towards the river.

The compass rose points about 69 degrees clockwise of up (magnetic north); the placement takes the direction of the modern road instead (about 96 degrees), and the bridge drawn on Highlands sheet 87 suggests about 74 to 82 degrees, so the rotation is uncertain by up to 15 degrees.

Printed sheet 72 of N.J. Coast vol. 1, Highland Beach (north end of the Sea Bright barrier at the Highlands bridge). Scale 60 ft to an inch. Ocean Av drawn horizontally in two strips with north to the right (compass about 69 degrees clockwise of up, magnetic). Three parts: 1 upper strip (Surf House, County Bridge, pavilions, bath houses, steam boat dock, Melrah Club); 2 inset at the upper left (The Neptune Boat Club, situated in the Highlands of Navesink, on the North Shrewsbury River); 3 lower strip (cottages, C.R.R. of N.J. passenger station and the Highlands branch trestle). The lower strip continues into the upper strip (match marks 72); its left end continues sheet 71 (navesink-1907). No cross streets survive: both strips are anchored on one hand-picked point.

Not georeferenced on this sheet: inset: The Neptune Boat Club, Highlands of Navesink (no street junction or shared feature with modern data; needs a placed Highlands river-front sheet showing the club, or a parcel corner identified on the shore).

sheet-72-3.description: The lower strip of sheet 72 of the 1907 New Jersey Coast volume shows Ocean Avenue on the Sea Bright barrier just south of Highland Beach, between the Shrewsbury River along the top and the Atlantic Ocean along the bottom; the sheet is turned so that north lies to the right. The river side of the avenue is a row of large summer cottages on deep lots running back to the shore, several with automobile houses and small piers on the river: the J. C. Duncan cottage with a balcony, Mrs. Barker's cottage, a cottage of J. B. Campbell, the Sand Bar Cottage and a second dwelling of S. Werver, Mrs. Murphy's house, and three more J. B. Campbell cottages numbered 2, 3 and 5. House numbers 2901 to 2907 are printed along the avenue and block number 183 in the row. On the ocean side, between the avenue and the bulkhead, run the tracks of the Central Railroad of New Jersey with the passenger station (number 2912). At the right the branch line to the Highlands leaves the main line in a long curve and crosses the river on a trestle. A six-inch water pipe runs in the avenue, which is marked 55 and 57 feet. The left end continues sheet 71 (Navesink Beach) and the right end continues into the upper strip of this sheet.
notes: Ocean Avenue is today's NJ 36; the railroad, the station and the Highlands branch trestle are gone.

Modern parcel lines on the river side at the Duncan / Barker and Barker / Campbell lot lines fall within about 3 m of the drawn ones through the placement, which supports the along-road position; the river frontage has since been filled and built over (condominiums).
Placed from one point carried from the upper strip at the match line marked 72, with the scale of the atlas's neighbours and the modern road direction; not checked against independent control.
